selected_news.source_headline: Cop31 left Chris Bowen stuck between petrostates and climate reality. But the f-word failure is not his alone
selected_news.article_text: Australia’s climate change minister will face a torrent of criticism over his role, but disagreement over fossil fuels proved an unbridgeable sticking point After delivering a major speech to the UN climate talks in Turkey last week, the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, dismissed criticisms that he hadn’t managed to name the problem that is overwhelmingly driving catastrophic global heating – burning fossil fuels “You could pick out any number of things that were not in what was a short speech,” he later said If Albanese really thought the head of a leading coal and gas exporter failing to address the issue head-on was inconsequential or trivial, then his climate change minister, Chris Bowen, will have a story for him after the finals days of the fractious talks that became the longest UN climate summit ever Those talks failed spectacularly to nail its prime ambition – an “Antalya pact” that was meant to drive investment in renewable energy and electrification, boost finance to help developing countries facing worsening climate damage, and acknowledge the world is bursting through a goal of limiting the increase in global temperatures to 1.5C, with alarming consequences across the planet As president of negotiations, Bowen barely slept for three days, and on the final night caught only a few moments of shut-eye on a couch in the office where a parade of negotiators had been coming to sit and talk to him Many of them raised a “red line” they said was non-negotiable – that any agreement from the summit must refer to the need for the world to “transition away from fossil fuels” that had previously been agreed at talks in Dubai three years ago. Others, including Saudi Arabia, didn’t want the words “fossil fuels” mentioned at all A compromise was proposed in the two final drafts of what was meant to be a “cover decision” – an overarching agreement that all countries would back. Drawn up by Bowen and his verbose Turkish counterpart, Cop31 president Murat Kurum, it suggested countries would “recall” the decision in Dubai “in its entirety” – effectively acknowledge its existence – but not say fossil fuels directly The European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Vanuatu, Norway and Belize were among the countries that said no. Ireland’s climate minister, Darragh O’Brien, said the omission was “unconscionable” and the EU could not support it. Climate campaigners agreed With the scheduled Friday finish of the summit a distant memory, Bowen left the stage of the plenary hall late on Sunday afternoon when it was clear too many countries could not accept the text that he had helped put on the table Speaking to journalists, Bowen said “Australia left nothing on the field” but the red lines he and his staff tried to negotiate were “unbridgeable”. In particular, the way a transition away from fossil fuels was mentioned Some countries said they couldn’t support a pact that didn’t mention it, and others “insisted if it was mentioned, they would veto”. “I would have been happy with transition away from fossil fuels being in the text, but that was not going to get support,” Bowen said Bowen said despite the breakdown, “in the real world” the transition away from fossil fuels was inevitable and irreversible – and happening at speed. A promised electrification target – that 35% of final energy will come from electricity by 2035, a step that analysis has found could significantly cut fossil fuel use – had the backing of more than 90 countries and was not a deal-breaker The climate minister will be presented with a torrent of criticism that the talks failed and he failed. Much domestic news coverage has focused on the cost of Cop31 to Australian taxpayers, rather than the substantive issues being dealt with In Antalya, the narrative out of the talks was quite different. Some said the rejection of the pact was a line in the sand that showed the world was no longer willing to accept lukewarm responses on the climate crisis that bent to the whims of fossil fuel interests and petrostates. Some nations are setting up voluntary pacts outside the UN negotiations to try to get the results they need Despite some claims in the dramatic final hours, the talks did not actually collapse. Many less controversial elements of the convention’s myriad processes were passed But the talks did fail to agree to the Antalya pact that Bowen and Kurum had spent so much political capital on. Some of this failure may be down to the Cop process itself – its reliance on consensus to pass agreements creates plenty of opportunities for countries to block and delay Luke Menzel, the chief executive of the Energy Efficiency Council, a membership group focused on electrification in Australia, was at the talks for the full two weeks. He says the reality is “this process has been fracturing for a long time” and had become much tougher after years of wars, rising geopolitical tension and a fuel price crisis caused by conflict in Iran “It turns out Antalya is where the conference finally fractured. In many ways it is remarkable we have had as many Cops as we have had in a row that have achieved a consensus,” he says Many climate experts and high-profile figures were left questioning whether the Cop process needs major revision. The former US vice-president and long-time climate campaigner Al Gore was among them, arguing it was “an outrage” that “a handful of petrostates have veto power over any mention of fossil fuels” and concluding “it has been clear for years that the Cop process is in need of significant reform” Some campaigners sharply criticised Australia’s role. Denise Cauchi, the chief executive of Climate Action Network Australia, said it had “failed to broker an agreement” and “caved” to the hundreds of lobbyists that were pushing for controversial carbon capture and storage technology to be promoted in the pact. Its attempted inclusion was seen as a sop to fossil fuel interests But some from Pacific nations, who see the breach of the 1.5C temperature goal as existential and whose interests Bowen had promised to champion, said the failure in Antalya is shared more widely In the chaotic final plenary session, the Fijian climate change minister, Lynda Tabuya, addressed Bowen directly as the rest of the world listened “You have tried your utmost best, and we have seen it. Your door has always been open,” she said. “This work is hard – sleepless nights, and over hours and days of constant negotiations. This is not easy but we do it and we do it for our people “The failure here is not yours to carry. It is the responsibility of all parties.”

selected_news.source_headline: Cop31 climate talks break down as key deal rejected
selected_news.article_text: EU, UK and some of developing world object to main text that ‘failed to meet the moment’ and did not mention fossil fuels The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels, in a dramatic finish to the Cop31 UN talks in Turkey The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required. [It] does not even mention fossil fuels.” As the talks, scheduled to end on Friday, dragged on into Sunday afternoon in the longest climate summit ever, it was clear that the “Antalya pact”, drafted by the Turkish and Australian joint presidencies of the summit, would not achieve the consensus needed to pass The Antalya pact invites countries to electrify their economies, calls for rich countries to provide finance to the poor to help them adapt to the impacts of the climate crisis, and calls on countries to minimise the “overshoot” of the 1.5C global heating threshold, of the Paris agreement But it failed to endorse the “transition away from fossil fuels” that more than 130 countries demanded, and included controversial provisions on “carbon capture and storage” (CCS) technology that some have said perpetuates fossil fuels The presidencies avoided outright collapse of the “conference of the parties” by passing decisions on various related matters, including the “just transition” to help workers in high-carbon industries shift to a low-carbon economy But Murat Kurum, Turkey’s Cop president, acknowledged there was no agreement on the draft “cover decision” text and so it had not been adopted “We have done our utmost; ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum ⁠such as a ‘take it or leave it’ demand,” he said. “It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise ⁠that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted.” Many countries, including the EU, UK and developing countries including small island states and some of the poorest countries, said they could not support the Antalya pact deal, which was supposed to be main outcome of the Cop In a dramatic intervention, O’Brien said on behalf of the EU that it could not accept the final text in its current form. “It fails to meet the moment … We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” He said the EU would not accept a decision “that greenwashes fossil fuels” His intervention was met by applause from the hall, and was later followed by similar objections from Panama, the Marshall Islands and Norway “This feels like a real line in the sand moment. Countries are standing up to fossil fuel interests and saying no,” said Bill Hare, the chief executive of the advisory group Climate Analytics But Mohamed Adow, the director of the thinktank Power Shift Africa, who called it “the worst Cop ever”, said: “The EU has rejected this text, but it cannot wash its hands of the wreckage it helped create ... For countries facing failed harvests, destroyed homes and mounting debt, this amounts to abandonment by the wealthy nations most responsible for the crisis “Europe’s hypocrisy is staggering. Its governments demand fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves.” Saudi Arabia defended the decision to include CCS in the text. Other countries, including the Africa group, China and Pakistan, also did not object to the deal, despite some having reservations. Pakistan told the conference that just because a few items in the pact were objectionable to some, the rest should not be sacrificed: “Climate action is not a menu from which we can select only what suits us.” Ghana also had criticisms of the process but did not reject the final text: “Africa has always chosen to build multilateralism rather than walk away from it.” Close to 200 countries have been meeting in Antalya for a fortnight under the joint presidencies of Turkey and Australia, with the overrunning talks marked by long periods of deadlock as countries failed to find common ground The Cop co-president, Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, defended his leadership. “Australia left nothing on the field,” he said, but the red lines the presidencies had tried to negotiate were “unbridgeable” Asked about the consensus-based system that broke down at the talks, Simon Stiell, the executive secretary of the UN framework convention on climate change, said: “It certainly fell short today,” while emphasising that a significant number of agenda items were passed, with “real progress and concrete results” But for many participants, these talks exposed a failure of collective will, particularly of the rich world, to confront the urgency of the climate crisis While extreme weather around the world has worsened this year, claiming tens of thousands of lives in heatwaves, in disasters such as the glacier collapse in Nepal, and in droughts and floods worsened by the supercharged El Niño, the slow speed of the climate negotiations appalled even veteran participants “There isn’t the sense of urgency to address these issues. That to me is very frustrating,” said Mary Robinson, a former president of Ireland and former UN climate envoy, as the talks neared their scheduled close. “We have co-presidents who haven’t really been stepping up and giving that leadership.” The UN secretary general, António Guterres, said: “I am deeply disappointed that Cop31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome. I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands. But this setback does not change the facts. There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science.”
